opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the intuition is pretty simple once you see it. Say you start with a randomly initialized policy playing against itself, in Go or chess or whatever, and you only train on the moves from games that ended in a win, basically behavior cloning on the winner's trajectory. The problem is that early on, a win between two random players carries almost no information. One random player beat another random player mostly by luck. So you're imitating a trajectory that's barely better than noise, and the policy doesn't get much signal about which moves actually mattered.

And then there's a deeper issue. In self-play, every game has a winner, so you always have "winning" data. That makes it feel like you're getting supervision, but the label "this side won" is relative to an opponent who is exactly as bad as you. You can end up reinforcing whatever quirks happened to correlate with winning in that particular population, and the policy can drift or collapse into a narrow set of strategies that beat itself but aren't actually good.

The other thing is credit assignment. A game might be two hundred moves long, and you're saying every move on the winning side was good. In reality maybe one or two moves decided the game and many of the rest were blunders the opponent failed to punish. Training only on winners throws away the contrast: you never see "this move led to a loss," so there's no gradient pushing you away from bad moves. You only get a positive signal, and it's very diluted.

That's why things like AlphaZero don't just clone winners. They use a value function trained on outcomes from both sides, plus search, to produce a much sharper target at every move. MCTS gives you an improved policy at each state, and that's what you distill, so the learning signal is dense and comes from both wins and losses. The naive version works in principle given enough samples, but the signal-to-noise ratio is terrible, especially at the start, and that's the crux of the problem.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is: if you only keep the winning games and throw away the losses, you've kind of thrown away half the information. In a two-player zero-sum game, every game has a winner, so by construction you're always going to have "winning" trajectories to train on. But the question is, what is the model actually learning from them?

If both copies of the policy are bad, one of them still wins. So you're imitating the winner of a contest between two bad players. The learning signal is relative, not absolute. You're not learning "this is good play," you're learning "this is slightly less bad than the other guy on this particular day." And that's fine early on, because that's basically how self-play bootstraps. But the signal gets noisier as the two policies converge, because when the players are evenly matched, who wins is dominated by luck, by sampling noise, by whatever stochasticity is in the environment. So you're doing behavior cloning on noise.

The other thing is you lose the contrast. The reason losses are useful is not that you want to avoid them per se, it's that the difference between the winning trajectory and the losing trajectory is where the information is. If you only see the winner's moves, you don't know which of those moves mattered. Most of the moves in a winning game were probably irrelevant, and some of them might have been actively bad, and the player got away with it. You're assigning credit uniformly to everything the winner did, and that's a very high-variance estimator of what's actually good.

So you get this kind of degenerate dynamic where the policy can drift. It can learn a quirk that happened to win against itself, then the opponent, which is the same network, learns the same quirk, and now neither side is punished for it. There's no external anchor. That's why people add things like value functions, or keep the losses with a negative weight, or maintain a league of past opponents, so the signal is grounded in something more than "I beat a copy of myself yesterday."

I'd frame it as: the naive version works, but it works more because of the structure of the game than because of the algorithm. You get a curriculum for free. What you don't get is a good gradient.

r001.rationale: The response calls the learning signal a “very high-variance estimator,” but does not state that gradient variance contains a term growing quadratically with game horizon T.

astra-6.text:
The problem is that winning is a property of the whole trajectory, but it doesn’t tell you which decisions were good. You can make a terrible move and still win because your opponent makes an even worse move. If you train on everything you did in winning games, you reinforce that terrible move too. And you throw away good moves that happened to occur in games you lost.

So there is a learning signal—moves that help you win should appear more often in winning games—but it’s noisy and depends on your opponent. Against a weak opponent, you can learn habits that work only because those mistakes aren’t punished. Self-play can improve that as the opponent improves, but filtering for wins alone doesn’t solve the credit-assignment problem.

sol-6.1.text:
The problem is that winning is a signal about the whole trajectory, but you’re using it to supervise every action in that trajectory. You might make a terrible move and then win because your opponent makes an even worse move. If you train on the winning game, you reinforce your terrible move, too. And conversely, you might play really well, make one mistake at the end, and throw away all the useful behavior in that losing game.

So self-play gives you an outcome signal, but it doesn’t automatically solve credit assignment. What you really want to know is whether a particular action improved your chances of winning relative to the alternatives. Just imitating the winner is a very noisy proxy for that.
